title: Writing a Menu
short: Balance the menu in methods, colors, richness and station load; describe dishes honestly; price from food cost; and look at what sells.
trouble: New chefs put five fried dishes on one menu, all from one overloaded station.

blocks.html: A menu is a promise to guests and a work plan for the kitchen. A good one balances both.

Balance the menu: a range of cooking methods, colors, textures, richness and prices, and spread the work across the stations. Describe dishes honestly and clearly; name what a guest needs to know (allergens, raw items). Price from cost: a common method divides the cost of one portion by the target food-cost percent (menu price = portion cost ÷ food-cost %). Menu analysis sorts dishes by how popular and how profitable they are, to decide what to keep, change or drop.

blocks.html: If five dishes come off the fryer and one off the grill, the fry cook drowns on a busy night while the grill cook waits. Balancing stations is as important as balancing flavors.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Write a five-dish dinner menu. Check it: are there at least three cooking methods? Are the stations balanced? Is every allergen clear?
